title: Supplying drinking water to Australian households

paragraphs.text: The importance of good drinking water in maintaining human health was recognised long ago. For example, water storage and treatment are mentioned in historical records dating back nearly 3,000 years. Australia is the driest continent in the world but even so, when Australians turn on their taps, they expect there to be water that flows at an acceptable pressure and that is available even when there has been no rainfall for months and the country is experiencing a drought. To meet these expectations, engineers designed and built urban water systems during the nineteenth and more particularly the twentieth century.

Most Australians live in urban areas and these are located in a water catchment area. Water catchments are the entire area from which streams and, in large catchment areas, rivers receive-or 'catch'- their water. Water catchment areas are surrounded by sloping ground, like hills or mountains. This means that drainage of water from the high ground to the lower levels of the catchment takes place naturally. The quality of the catchment determines the quality of the water that is supplied from it. In a few highly protected areas, catchments exist in their natural state and minimal water treatment is needed. For example, most of the water supply for the cities of Melbourne and Canberra comes from natural wilderness catchments which have been set aside solely for this purpose.

Only a few other communities, however, have such excellent unspoiled water sources. For example, most of the city of Adelaide's water is derived from the Murray River, which has a vast catchment area with a population of almost two million people, and contains more than 50,000 farms. The use of land for agricultural purposes means that water supplies from this catchment area could contain material that could pollute the water. As a result, the water needs treatment. Where there are no natural catchment areas, the water supply may be obtained by damming rivers and storing the water in reservoirs.

An additional source of water is groundwater, or water which is found underground. Australia has one of the largest naturally occurring underground water stores in the world: the Great Artesian Basin (GAB). The GAB holds enough water to cover the Earth's landmass to a depth of half a metre, but it is not an underground lake. The GAB is made up of layers of rock and the water is stored in the sand that fills the spaces between the vast rock layers. Although water is constantly leaking into the GAB from rainfall and rivers, the majority of the drinking water that is obtained from the GAB has been there for 1 to 2 million years. Water emerges naturally from the GAB through faults or vents into springs or shallow water tables, or leaks slowly through layers of rock to the naturally more than a century, holes have been drilled into the rock of the GAB and water has been pumped out for domestic and agricultural use.

Before it is piped to homes, all water undergoes some form of treatment to get rid of sediments and to kill potentially harmful microorganisms. Chlorine is the most widely used disinfectant for drinking water in Australia. It is cheap, easy to use, and effective against a wide range of microorganisms; chlorine also has a long history of safe use around the world.

In Australia, the states and territories are largely responsible for protecting public health and managing natural resources, including water supplies. There are, however, some households in rural areas that are so remote that it is too expensive for authorities to connect them to the water supply. Instead, these households get their water from rainwater collected off their house roofs and stored in large water tanks. Outside major cities there can be as many as one in four households that rely on rainwater stored in tanks for all their domestic water needs.

Rainwater tanks are well established in rural Australia, but during the drought of 2003 to 2010 the value of rainwater tanks to supplement the water needs of urban residents was recognised. This resulted in the installation of rainwater tanks becoming compulsory for new buildings in some cities. Some state governments pay for rainwater tanks in areas where they are considered an important means of increasing the water supply. Rainwater is not treated with chlorine, and there has been some concern that airborne dirt, which settles onto rooftops, may be a health risk in urban or industrial areas. However, reports of illness associated with rainwater tanks are rare, and public health studies in South Australia (the Australian state with the highest rainwater usage rate) have not identified a connection between water-borne illnesses and the use of rainwater tanks.
